title: Diesel Care During Winter
description: Practical winter diesel maintenance tips for Colorado drivers, from batteries and fuel filters to glow plugs, coolant and the right oil.
author: Robert McKay
body: Winter is tough on diesel engines, and preventive maintenance becomes even more important when temperatures drop. A few checks before the first hard freeze can prevent a no-start, protect the fuel system and make the truck more dependable all season.
Cold weather can expose a restricted or overdue fuel filter quickly. Keeping the filter in good condition helps maintain fuel flow and reduces the chance of hard starts or stalling.
2. Use fuel suited for winter conditions

Diesel fuel can gel when temperatures fall far enough. Buy fuel from a high-volume station and follow the vehicle and fuel supplier guidance for winterized fuel or anti-gel treatment when conditions call for it.
Cold weather reduces available battery power while a cold diesel engine needs plenty of cranking speed. Test weak batteries before winter and keep terminals clean and tight.
Coolant protects against both overheating and freezing. Check level, condition, leaks and freeze protection before winter, especially on a work truck that sees long drives or towing.
Oil that is too thick for the temperature can make cold starts harder. Use the viscosity and specification recommended for the engine and climate.
6. Pay attention to glow-plug or intake-heater performance
If cold starts are getting longer, rougher or smokier, the starting-aid system deserves a look before the coldest mornings arrive.
Air pressure drops as temperatures fall. Proper inflation and healthy tread help with braking, handling and fuel economy on cold Colorado roads.
If your diesel is hard to start, losing power or simply due for winter maintenance, schedule a visit and McKay's Garage can help you get ahead of it.

title: Your Ultimate Pre-Purchase Inspection Guide
description: Why a pre-purchase vehicle inspection can reveal hidden problems and help you make a better used-car decision before money changes hands.
author: Stephen Smith
body: A used vehicle can look great in a listing and still be hiding expensive problems. A pre-purchase inspection gives you an independent mechanical look at the vehicle before you commit.

The goal is not to find a perfect used vehicle. It is to understand what you are buying. Existing leaks, worn suspension, brake concerns, warning codes, maintenance needs and signs of prior damage can all change whether the asking price makes sense.

A useful inspection looks beyond the paint. The engine, transmission and drivetrain, brakes, steering, suspension, tires, fluids, electrical systems and visible underbody condition should all be considered. A scan can also reveal stored diagnostic information that may not be obvious during a short test drive.
Use the results to make a decision

An inspection gives you information. You may decide the vehicle is a good fit, negotiate based on upcoming work, or walk away from a repair bill you did not want. Any of those outcomes can save money and stress.

title: Check Engine Light On? What Longmont Drivers Should Do Next
description: A check-engine light is a clue, not a parts list. Learn what solid automotive diagnostics should include before you approve a repair.
author: McKay's Garage
body: The check-engine light has an annoying habit of showing up when the vehicle still feels completely normal. Other times it appears right along with rough running, low power, hard starting or poor fuel economy. Either way, the light is telling you the computer saw something outside the expected range.
A trouble code is the beginning of the diagnosis

Plugging in a scan tool is useful, but the code rarely means 'replace this exact part.' A code identifies a system, circuit or operating condition. The next step is verifying what caused it with live data, visual inspection, electrical tests or mechanical checks.
Flashing and steady lights are different

A steady light usually means the vehicle needs diagnosis soon. A flashing check-engine light can indicate an active misfire that may damage the catalytic converter. If the vehicle is shaking, losing power, overheating or showing oil-pressure warnings, stop driving and get advice before continuing.

Replacing a sensor because its name appears in a code description can miss vacuum leaks, damaged wiring, fuel-delivery problems or another component that caused the sensor reading to look wrong. Testing first helps avoid paying for parts that did not solve the problem.

Write down when the light appeared, whether the engine was cold or warm, road speed, fuel level, recent repairs and any noises or drivability changes. Those details can shorten the path to the real cause.

title: Diesel Truck Maintenance in Colorado: What Towing, Altitude and Weather Change
description: Colorado diesel trucks often tow, climb and face big temperature swings. Here is how those conditions change the way you should think about maintenance.
author: McKay's Garage
body: A diesel pickup that spends its life commuting on flat roads has an easier job than a truck pulling a trailer up I-70, idling at a jobsite or starting on a zero-degree morning. Colorado use can turn a normal maintenance schedule into severe service in a hurry.
Heavy towing loads the cooling system, engine oil, transmission and differentials. Fluid condition and cooling-system health matter because heat is one of the fastest ways to shorten component life.
Short trips can be hard on modern diesels

Many emissions systems work best when the engine reaches full operating temperature for enough time. Constant short trips and extended idling can create different maintenance needs than steady highway driving.
Altitude changes how hard the truck works

Turbocharged diesels compensate well for altitude, but long grades still create sustained load. Pay attention to unusual boost behavior, rising temperatures, new smoke, reduced power or changes in fuel economy.
Cold weather tests batteries and fuel systems

A weak battery that seemed fine in summer may fail on the first truly cold morning. Fuel filters, glow-plug or intake-heater systems, winter fuel quality and the correct oil all become more important when temperatures drop.
Maintenance should match the way you use the truck
Mileage alone does not tell the whole story. Towing weight, idle hours, trip length, age and service history all matter. A practical maintenance plan looks at the actual truck and its job.

title: 7 Signs Your Steering or Suspension Needs Attention
description: Clunks, wandering, vibration and uneven tire wear can point to steering or suspension wear. Learn the symptoms that deserve an inspection.
author: McKay's Garage
body: Steering and suspension parts wear gradually, which means drivers often adapt to a vehicle that no longer handles the way it should. By the time the change feels dramatic, a tire or another component may already be paying the price.
Loose ball joints, sway-bar links, control-arm bushings, strut mounts and other components can make knocking or clunking sounds as the suspension moves.
If you are constantly correcting the steering on a straight road, worn steering parts, alignment, tire issues or suspension wear may be involved.
Feathering, cupping or one-sided wear can be a clue that the tire is not staying planted correctly. Do not assume an alignment alone will fix wear caused by loose components.
Extra play, delayed response or a steering wheel that feels vague deserves an inspection because tie rods, ball joints, steering gear and other parts affect vehicle control.
Worn shocks and struts can reduce control over body movement, especially over dips, during braking or on rough roads.
Vibration can come from tires, wheel bearings, driveline components or suspension issues. Where and when you feel it helps narrow the source.
7. A lift kit changed the way the vehicle drives
Changing ride height changes geometry. If a lifted truck pulls, wears tires quickly or feels unstable, the installation and related steering and suspension components should be checked.

title: Transmission Service vs. Transmission Rebuild: How to Know What You Actually Need
description: A slipping or rough-shifting transmission does not automatically need a rebuild. Learn why diagnosis comes before the repair decision.
author: McKay's Garage
body: Few automotive words create a bigger pit in your stomach than 'transmission.' The good news is that a shift problem does not automatically mean the transmission has to come out of the vehicle.
Slipping, delayed engagement, harsh shifts, shuddering, leaks, noises and warning lights can have different causes. Modern transmissions also depend heavily on electrical controls and sensor data.

If the transmission is operating normally and the vehicle is due for maintenance, the correct fluid and filter service may be all that is needed. Service is preventive maintenance, not a cure-all for internal damage.
When diagnosis is more important than a fluid change

If the unit is already slipping, making noise or setting codes, it should be evaluated before anyone promises that fresh fluid will fix it. Fluid condition, line pressure, controls and mechanical operation may all need to be considered.
A rebuild becomes a realistic option when internal clutches, bearings, seals or hard parts are worn or damaged and the rest of the vehicle justifies the investment.
Do not forget the rest of the drivetrain
Differentials, transfer cases, driveshafts and wheel bearings can create noises or vibrations that drivers sometimes blame on the transmission. A good inspection looks at the whole system.

title: How Often Should You Change Your Oil in Colorado?
description: Oil-change intervals depend on more than mileage. Learn how short trips, towing, cold starts and engine age can change the answer.
author: McKay's Garage
body: There is no single oil-change interval that is right for every vehicle. Modern engines, oil specifications and maintenance monitors have changed the old one-size-fits-all advice, but the way you drive still matters.
Your owner's manual and maintenance monitor are the baseline. Use the oil viscosity and specification the engine was designed for rather than choosing only by brand or price.
Severe use can shorten the interval
Frequent short trips, towing, long idle time, dusty roads, very cold starts and repeated mountain driving can be harder on oil than steady highway miles.
Leaks, oil consumption and engine condition matter. Checking the level between services is especially important on an older engine that uses some oil.
Maintenance is also an inspection opportunity
An oil service is a good time to notice fluid leaks, tire wear, loose steering components or other changes before they become a breakdown.

title: Battery, Alternator or Wiring? How Automotive Electrical Problems Get Diagnosed
description: Slow cranking, dead batteries and warning lights can have several causes. Learn how a real charging-system and electrical diagnosis narrows it down.
author: McKay's Garage
body: A dead battery does not always mean the battery is the problem. A weak alternator, poor cable connection, parasitic draw, damaged wiring or a module that never goes to sleep can leave you with the same symptom.
Voltage by itself does not tell the whole story. A battery can show reasonable voltage and still fail to deliver enough current when the starter asks for it.
The alternator needs to supply the vehicle and recharge the battery, but modern charging strategies vary. Testing should account for the way that specific vehicle controls charging.
Voltage drop can reveal bad connections
Corrosion or resistance in battery cables and grounds can cause slow cranking, strange electrical behavior or charging problems even when major components test well.
If a good battery goes dead after the vehicle sits, current may be flowing when it should not. Finding the circuit requires measuring the draw and narrowing down what stays awake.

title: Prepare Your Diesel Truck for a Colorado Winter Before the First Hard Freeze
description: A practical pre-winter diesel checklist for batteries, fuel, filters, coolant, oil, glow-plug systems and tires.
author: McKay's Garage
body: Colorado weather can go from mild afternoons to freezing mornings fast. A diesel that starts easily in September can show every weak spot in the system once overnight temperatures plunge.
Test both batteries if the truck uses a pair
Matched battery pairs need to work together. One weak battery can pull the system down and make cranking slower when cold oil already makes the engine harder to turn.
Take fuel and filter condition seriously
Replace an overdue fuel filter and buy fresh fuel from busy stations. Follow appropriate winter-fuel guidance for the temperatures you expect.
Glow plugs, intake heaters and their control systems should work before you depend on them. Longer crank time or rough white-smoke starts can be an early clue.
Check coolant freeze protection and leaks
A proper coolant mixture protects from freezing and corrosion. Small leaks are easier to address before winter than on a cold roadside.
Use the correct oil and watch tire pressure
Correct cold-weather oil helps cranking, and tire pressure naturally falls as the air temperature drops. Both are simple items with a big impact on winter reliability.

title: Lift Kits, Suspension Geometry and Tire Wear: What Changes After You Raise a Truck
description: Lifting a truck changes more than appearance. Learn how suspension geometry, steering angles and tire wear should be considered after installation.
author: McKay's Garage
body: A lift kit can add clearance and change the stance of a truck, but it also changes the working angles of suspension and steering components. The best setup is one that matches the truck's actual use, not just the number on the box.
Camber, caster and toe can all be affected depending on the suspension design and amount of lift. Correcting those angles is important for handling and tire life.
Tie-rod, ball-joint and CV axle angles may become steeper. Excessive angles can increase wear or create binding, vibration and handling changes.
Bigger tires add their own load
Heavier wheels and tires change leverage on bearings, steering and brakes. Gearing and drivability can also feel different as tire diameter increases.
After components settle, it is smart to recheck fasteners, tire wear and alignment. New noises or wandering should be investigated rather than accepted as normal.
